# Execution: the stage executor and CUDA graphs {#sec-ch11}

The earlier chapters describe what one stage computes. This chapter describes how a stage is run. A block's
stage is a short list of operations: the stage-entry exchange, the advance (fluxes, sources and the implicit
correction), the user forcing, the Runge–Kutta combine, the saturation adjustment, the chemistry step and the
ghost fill. The stage executor groups that list into segments and runs each segment in one of two ways: eagerly,
launching every kernel from the host as the code reaches it, or as a CUDA[^rg-df3b18643faf] graph, captured once and then replayed
as a single launch. Both ways compute the same bits; the graph saves the cost of issuing the kernels one by one.

@sec-ch11-segments gives the schedule and its segments. @sec-ch11-capture describes how a segment is captured
and replayed, and what is saved and restored around the capture. @sec-ch11-refusals lists the reasons a block
runs eager instead, and @sec-ch11-default the deck keys that choose the execution and make a refusal an error.
@sec-ch11-graphsafe gives the rules a kernel must follow to run inside a graph, and the device step that lets
one capture serve every step size. @sec-ch11-s4 says what the eager path costs and where that cost is measured,
and @sec-ch11-eagerops how an operation that cannot be captured runs between captured segments. A Mesh of several
blocks captures its blocks together; the exchange cuts and the agreement rule are @sec-ch13. How a test run under
the default execution is classified is @sec-ch16-capture.
